extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate media studies students and instructors (introductory political economy of media)
extracted.subtask_description: Using Chomsky and Herman's Propaganda Model to analyze how structural and economic factors shape mass-media content and bias; identifying the model's filters, limits, and complementary approaches. Suitable for classroom/media-analysis assignments and critical reading of news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of mass media (propaganda role)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mass media serve as a system for communicating messages and symbols to the general populace. It is their function to amuse, entertain, and inform, and to inculcate individuals with the values, beliefs, and codes of behaviour that will integrate them into the institutional structures of the larger society. In a world of concentrated wealth and major conflicts of class interest, to fulfil this role requires systematic propaganda." (Chomsky and Herman 1988:1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the starting evaluative premise: ask whether media content serves to naturalise ruling-class ideology and integrate audiences into existing institutions rather than fostering critical public debate. Examples/diagnostics include consistent framing aligning with elite interests, selective coverage, and privileging of establishment narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 1: Size and ownership of mass media corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The size and ownership of mass media corporations"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine concentration of ownership, conglomeration, and cross-ownership links; consider how corporate structures and ownership stakes might constrain editorial lines, set agendas, or limit dissenting perspectives. Look for corporate influence in staffing, resource allocation, and strategic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 2: Economic model based on corporate advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: "The economic model predicated on generating revenue via corporate advertising"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how dependence on advertising revenue shapes content choices: avoidance of advertiser-hostile topics, favourable coverage of advertiser interests, and prioritisation of mass-appeal formats. Consider alternative revenue models and whether they enable more independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 3: Reliance on 'trusted sources' (government/corporate spokespeople)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reliance on ‘trusted sources’ which frequently means using government or corporate spokespeople who spend vast sums on public relations and lobbying"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sourcing patterns: frequency of official/government/corporate sources vs. independent experts or affected communities; uncritical relay of press releases; embedded reliance on institutional PR as legitimate news input. Anti-pattern: treating press offices as neutral truth-providers without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 4: Flak — privileged actors' ability to respond negatively
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ability of financially or politically privileged actors to provide flak, negative responses to critical media coverage"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify mechanisms of flak (lawsuits, advertiser pressure, coordinated rebuttals, political complaints) and whether they deter critical reporting. Evaluate editorial responses to flak and whether fear of sanction narrows permissible discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 5: Ideological filter (anticommunism / dominant ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An ideological filter described as anticommunism (due to Manufacturing Consent being published during the final years of the Cold war)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ideological filter by checking pervasive hostile/reductive framings of particular ideologies or movements; note the model's historical update—anticommunism may be replaced by 'war on terror' or more generally a 'dominant ideology'. Use this to trace consistent normative assumptions that exclude or delegitimise alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological filter evolution and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent analyses suggest the ideological filter persists but may be rebranded (e.g., war on terror replacing anticommunism; Klaehn's 'dominant ideology').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the PM historically or cross-nationally, look for the locally salient ideological discourses that function like anticommunism did in the Cold War (e.g., national security narratives). Don't treat the specific label as fixed; identify the role rather than the exact terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across media systems (US origin, modifiable for Europe)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the PM was designed with specific reference to media in the USA, subsequent studies suggest that with minor modifications the PM can be adapted for use with European style mass media systems which include a public service broadcaster element alongside a commercial media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural differences (public-service broadcasting, regulatory frameworks) when applying the model; modify expectations about dominance of commercial imperatives and examine how public-service institutions might mitigate or reproduce filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and caveats of the Propaganda Model
rubrics_metrics.description: Chomsky and Herman do not claim that the PM captures all factors which influence mass media coverage, or that the filters preclude significant differentiations within and between media conglomerates; there are short periods where specific historic and/or social circumstances open limited windows of opportunity for journalists to engage in less constrained critiques of powerful actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the PM as a diagnostic lens, not a deterministic formula. In evaluation, allow for heterogeneity across outlets, temporal changes, and instances of critical reporting. Beware over-deterministic readings that ignore agency, journalistic contestation, and contingent contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential and limits of alternative media / new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the new technologies have great potential for democratic communication, there is little reason to expect the Internet to serve democratic ends if it is left to the market. (Herman 2000)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing digital/alternative media, weigh their democratizing potential against market pressures, ownership of platforms, algorithmic amplification, and commercialization. Do not assume online equals democratic; interrogate economic and infrastructural constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary approaches: audience/reception studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative approaches, which concentrate on the processes by which audiences create meaning from media texts can be found in reception studies, audience studies and strands of cultural studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include audience decoding, interpretive diversity, and cultural context as part of evaluation—measure how audiences reinterpret or resist elite framings. Use PE and reception approaches as complementary: structural production-side analysis plus consumption-side analysis for fuller understanding.
